summary: Updates the eligibility rules for volunteering for the IETF Nominating Committee, in light of the fully online meetings of 2020 and 2021. It adjusts how meeting participation counts toward eligibility compared with RFC 8713.

plainLanguage.summary: The group that picks leaders had rules about attending meetings in person. After online meetings became normal, the rules were adjusted.

questions: can online meetings count for nomcom
who can volunteer for the ietf nomcom
can remote attendance count for nomcom eligibility
subtitle: Who may volunteer for the IETF's Nominating Committee once meetings can be attended online.

tldr.problem: The Nominating Committee (NomCom) picks IETF leaders from randomly selected volunteers, but the old rule of attending three of the last five meetings meant in person, which no longer fitted a community that often meets online.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9389 replaces the attendance text of RFC 8713 with three alternative paths to eligibility: attending meetings in person or online, chairing or being secretary of a working group, or authoring at least two IETF Stream RFCs.
tldr.outcome: It makes the rules of the earlier online-era experiment permanent, obsoletes RFC 8788 and RFC 8989, and openly weighs the new risk of NomCom capture and disruptive volunteers.

facts.label: Path 1
facts.value: 3 of the last 5 meetings, in person or online

facts.label: Path 2
facts.value: WG Chair or Secretary within 3 years

facts.label: Path 3
facts.value: At least 2 IETF Stream RFCs within 5 years

facts.label: Capture threshold
facts.value: 6 or more of the NomCom seats

today: RFC 9389 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10 with RFC 8713) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 8788 and RFC 8989, and it updates RFC 8713, whose eligibility text it replaces.

sections.title: Why the Rules Needed Changing
sections.content:
The Nominating Committee (NomCom) nominates a single candidate for each open seat on the IAB, the IESG, the IETF Trust and the IETF LLC Board. RFC 8713 defines how it works. NomCom voting members are chosen at random from a pool of volunteers, so it matters that the pool is made up of people who know how the IETF operates.

Section 4.14 of RFC 8713 required volunteers to have attended three of the previous five meetings. In practice that meant picking up a badge at an in-person meeting. After six consecutive fully online meetings in 2020 and 2021, that reading would have left no eligible volunteers. RFC 8989 therefore ran an experiment that also counted logging in to an online meeting.

RFC 9389 uses the experiment's criteria to replace the attendance text in the first two paragraphs of Section 4.14 of RFC 8713. It obsoletes RFC 8989, and it also obsoletes RFC 8788, which set rules only for the 2020-2021 NomCom. All other text in RFC 8713 stays as it was.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone started joining meetings from home, the old rule about showing up in person stopped making sense. This document writes down a new rule that works for both.

sections.title: NomCom Principles
sections.content:
The RFC starts from first principles. NomCom is meant to be a random sample of "the community." For years, in-person attendance was a fair proxy for commitment, because two days of travel and an attendance fee is a large spend of time and money. It was also thought to build familiarity with candidates, although nothing ensured any interaction.

Two principles drive the design. The community should govern itself, so volunteers need a demonstrated commitment to the IETF. And limiting how many volunteers one organization sponsors avoids mischief that could disrupt operations or work against the community as a whole.

Remote attendance lowers the barrier. The IETF has historically offered a fee-free remote option, so the only investment is logging on once per meeting, sometimes at an inconvenient local hour. The RFC notes that overly restrictive criteria also work against a broad talent pool, and that admitting remote-only attendees is likely to require a remote component in NomCom operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The lottery should draw from people who really care about the club. Showing up used to prove that, but joining online is a fair way to show it too, and it lets more people in.

sections.title: The Three Eligibility Paths
sections.content:
A person must satisfy one of three paths to volunteer, and any one is enough unless they are disqualified under Section 4.15 of RFC 8713.

  • Path 1: registered for and attended three out of the last five IETF meetings, in person or online. In-person attendance is taken from the Secretariat's records. Online attendance means a registered person who logged in for at least one session of the meeting.
  • Path 2: served as a Working Group Chair or Secretary within the three years before the day the call for NomCom volunteers is sent.
  • Path 3: listed as an author or editor on the front page of at least two IETF Stream RFCs within the five years before that day.

For Path 3, an Internet-Draft approved by the IESG and sitting in the RFC Editor queue counts like a published RFC, dated from when it entered the queue. The five-year timer runs back from the date the call for volunteers is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to get your name in the lottery: come to enough meetings, run a working group, or write at least two RFCs. Any one of them is enough.

sections.title: NomCom Capture
sections.content:
The main threat is that an organization, or a group of coordinating ones, obtains a majority of NomCom seats to steer the IETF leadership toward a self-serving agenda. RFC 8713 lets the NomCom Chair set the voting requirement, but seven of ten forms a quorum, so at worst seven members working together can almost certainly impose their will.

Counting remote attendance cuts the minimum cost of making one eligible volunteer from three in-person trips of around five days each over at least eight months to no financial cost and the time to log in three times over at least eight months.

Three things work against an attacker. First, a surge of volunteers dilutes them: with 300 legitimate volunteers, an attacker needs 365 to exceed a 50% chance of controlling six or more of the ten seats. A sudden unexplained surge is also an early warning sign. Second, the two-per-organization limit from Section 4.17 of RFC 8713 forces the attacker to coordinate several organizations, bribe others or invent affiliations; with 300 legitimate volunteers from different organizations, three conspiring organizations would need 771 volunteers (257 each). Third, the three-meeting wait of at least eight months means an attack must be visible for a year, giving leadership months to react.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone might try to stuff the lottery with their friends so they win most of the spots. The rules make that hard: it takes lots of fake entries, there is a limit per company, and it takes months of waiting where people can notice.

sections.title: Disruptive Candidates and Remedies
sections.content:
Remote attendance also lets a single person mount an attack that once needed coordination. By registering remotely under several identities over a year, one individual can make each identity eligible and serve under whichever is selected, then try to disrupt or stall the NomCom's work, or merely improve their odds of being picked. This is harder to detect than coordinated attacks. The lower cost of remote participation makes it more feasible, although the attacker cannot be sure of fee waivers for every identity.

The existing defence is the voting member recall procedure in Section 5.7 of RFC 8713, which allows removal and replacement of disruptive members.

Further changes are out of scope, but the RFC suggests two ideas. One is a challenge process against volunteers with a suspicious reported affiliation or who might be aliases of one person. The other is letting challenges to the random selection (Section 4.17 of RFC 8713) cover the data used to qualify a volunteer, not only the randomization.
sections.plainLanguage: One sneaky person could sign up under many names. The club can already remove troublemakers, and could add a way for people to challenge suspicious names.

sections.title: The Capture Mathematics
sections.content:
Appendix A shows the working behind the numbers. Let L be the legitimate volunteers and A the attacking volunteers. The NomCom has ten voting members, and capture means attackers win six or more seats. The chance is a sum of combinations, divided by the total ways to choose ten members from L plus A. For L = 300 it crosses 50% at A = 365.

With the two-per-organization limit, the appendix assumes the 300 legitimate volunteers all come from different organizations, which it calls unfavorable to the attacker, and three conspiring organizations so that no more than six members can come from the attackers. Under those assumptions the attackers need A = 771 to pass a 50% chance of capture.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors counted all the ways the lottery could turn out to see how many fake entries an attacker would need. The answer was a very large number.
